Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

contextLabel.description: Short header tying the suggestion to the user request.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

keywords.description: Topic keywords from the user's request.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__batch
tools.description: Create a doc, or apply several operations to one doc atomically.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__guide
tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__start_session
tools.description:
Start a separate Claude Code session for a task while you stay with the user (when: see "Starting other sessions"). `initiation` says who wants it: "user_asked" starts it now and returns its id; "offer" is for a task the user named in their latest message (new work here, or "suggest / split off / make a task or session for X"): called with a title alone, it shows a "New session" / "Do it here" card and WAITS for their answer, so it must be the only call in that message (no update_plan, no other tool); the result then tells you to carry on here, or to send the brief with proposal_id so the session starts; "own_initiative" is for work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up (when your reply calls work a follow-up or a separate PR, propose it here rather than only saying so, unless it acts on what this session just found and so stays here), never what "Starting other sessions" keeps here or gives to a subagent; the user sees a card and nothing runs until they start it, by clicking it or by telling you (then call this again with just proposal_id).
"user_asked" and "own_initiative" both need a `prompt` — the brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like — and the call is refused without it; `background` does not stand in for it. Only an "offer" is a title alone.
context: "fork" = this whole conversation + your `prompt`. "fresh" (default) = your `prompt` + `background` only, so `background` is required too, at least 80 characters.
Checkout here ("fresh" only): use_worktree false = shares this checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session its branch and PR too: never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); true = its own worktree (the default when this session is in one).
Elsewhere ("fresh", user_asked only, when the user named the place): `cwd`, `target` "ssh" + `host`, `environment` or `preset`; list_start_targets lists the valid names.

initiation.description: "user_asked": the user asked in words for separate, parallel or background work, or told you to start this piece — it starts now (not for a piece "Starting other sessions" gives to a subagent). "offer": a task the user named in their latest message (new work for this session, or one they asked you to suggest, split off or make a session for) — the user is asked first and the call waits for their answer; send only title with it (the brief follows, with proposal_id, if they choose New session). "own_initiative": work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up; it waits as a proposal card until the user starts it; never for a task the user's message tells you to do, nor for the one piece of work "Starting other sessions" keeps here, nor for what it gives to a subagent. Required unless proposal_id is set.

proposal_id.description: Start a proposal the user told you to start, exactly as proposed: its task_id and nothing else (wake_when_done may accompany a local one). To change it, dismiss_task it and start a new session.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task. Shown on the row or card. Required unless proposal_id is set.

prompt.description: The brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like. Required for "user_asked" and "own_initiative" — the call is refused without it, and `background` does not stand in for it; an "offer" leaves it out (the card shows the user's own message) and you send it with proposal_id once they choose New session. Here and in `background`, put file paths and code identifiers in backticks.

context.description: "fresh" (default) or "fork" — see the tool description. A "fork" from a worktree session gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip (commit first; uncommitted edits stay here); from a plain checkout it shares the folder.

background.description: Required with "fresh", besides `prompt`: at least 80 characters of overall goal, decisions and constraints so far, how this piece fits — for someone who has not seen this conversation. Ignored for "fork".

wake_when_done.description: Once this session (and any sibling still working) ends its turn, or fails to start (unless it waits at a prompt the user answers there, its folder was never opened in Claude Desktop, or the user started, stopped or archived it), and you are idle, the app continues you, whether or not this is set. true also continues you if this session never gets its task some other way, such as a brief that is not sent; default false; not with own_initiative; ignored with target "cloud", which never continues you.

name.description: Optional short handle for the session ([a-z0-9-], ≤24), e.g. "cli-cleanup". Linked sessions and plan steps refer to it by this name; derived from the title when omitted.

use_worktree.description: "fresh" only (rejected with "fork"). false = shares this session's checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session: its worktree, branch and PR, so never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); not accepted from a session set up to move from the user's checkout into a worktree with EnterWorktree (before or after it moves), a fork of a session working in a worktree on an SSH host, or one whose worktree was given back. At another place named by `cwd`, `host` or `preset`, false = that folder as it is. true = its own git worktree. Omitted: the same folder when this session works in a plain folder and has never had a worktree (its own, a shared one, or one it will enter later); otherwise its own worktree. Omitted with `preset` or `host`, or with `cwd` from a session on an SSH host: the default set on that preset or SSH connection instead.

model.description: "fresh" only, optional: a cheaper model id for mechanical or read-only pieces (e.g. a Sonnet or Haiku id). Same family or cheaper than yours; anything higher is ignored. Omit to inherit yours.

target.description: "fresh" only. "local" (default) = where this session runs. "cloud" = run it as a cloud session (keeps going when this computer sleeps). Needs the repository on GitHub and a cloud environment — the app checks and tells the user if it cannot, and the task then stays as a card for them to start. model/effort/use_worktree/cwd/source_branch do not apply. Only when the user asks for the cloud. "ssh" = on the SSH connection named by host (or by a preset).

host.description: With target "ssh": the name of one of the user's saved SSH connections (as list_start_targets reports it) — never a raw hostname, user or key. The app connects as the user configured it and may ask them to sign in.

cwd.description: The folder the session works in, when it is not this project: an absolute (or ~/) path on the host it will run on — this computer, this session's host, or the SSH connection named by host (default there: the connection's folder). "fresh" only.

environment.description: With target "cloud": the name or id of one of the user's cloud environments (list_start_targets lists them); omitted = the default one.

repository.description: With target "cloud", only when the user named a repository other than this project's: "owner/name" on github.com, which the cloud session clones at its default branch. Take the exact owner/name from the user's words or a listing that shows it; if you are not sure of it, ask them. A bypass or auto permission mode may not carry over: the session then starts in the cloud's default mode. If the call is refused, do not run or propose the other repository's work in this project.

source_branch.description: The existing local branch the new worktree is cut from. Default in this project: this session's base branch (the one picked when it started, or the one its worktree was cut from). If the session has none and either it runs on an SSH host or its project folder is itself a git worktree or submodule, the folder's current commit. Otherwise, the repository's default branch, or the folder's current commit if that is unknown. Only for a session that gets its own worktree (use_worktree true, or the place's default); not with target "cloud".

branch_name.description: A short slug for the new worktree's branch (the app adds the user's branch prefix and a suffix). Only with a worktree.

preset.description: The name of one of the user's saved session presets on this computer: it names the place itself (a folder here or an SSH connection and folder — do not pass host or cwd with it) and brings model, effort and worktree defaults plus its saved environment variables; use_worktree/model/effort override those. Cloud and Remote Control presets are not available here.

effort.description: "fresh" only, optional: reasoning effort at or below yours. Omit to inherit.

permission_mode.description: Optional, local starts only: the permission mode it starts in — this session's own or a lower one (omit to inherit it). A higher mode, or one the app does not offer here, is refused; raising a session is set_session_permission_mode's card to show.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). The search turned up mostly 2026 coverage, with the 2025 change visible in a few sources.

- **The 2025 shift:** Several guides date the move from flat per-message pricing to complexity-weighted credit pricing to July 2025. One source describes the earlier setup as 1 credit = 1 interaction.
- **Messages vs. credits:** One guide says Lovable switched from "messages" to credits and that the change makes costs clearer. Its example is about 2 credits for a landing-page generation versus 0.5 for a small edit (automationatlas.io).
- **Current structure (2026):** Chat usage now has its own pricing, with a per-message price and a daily chat allowance, separate from build credits. Lovable's docs state this, and the source dates the change to October 2026 (usagepricing.com; docs.lovable.dev). Another source says that before August 2026, build credits, Cloud usage, and AI gateway usage were billed separately, and a single credit balance now covers all three (rapidevelopers.com).
- **Free tier:** Sources disagree on the free allowance. Some describe 5 daily build credits that reset and don't roll over (rapidevelopers.com), and others describe 5 messages per day with no rollover (lowcode.agency).
- **Prices:** Most recent sources list Pro at $25/month and Business at $50/month. One older comparison lists Pro at $21 (websitebuilderexpert.com).

Caveat: the sources are mostly third-party blogs and some have inconsistent dates. Lovable's own docs (docs.lovable.dev/user-guides/credits) are the authoritative reference for current terms.

Both precedents checked. GitHub Copilot named its unit after the expensive thing, "premium requests", gave each model a multiplier up to 20×, and has since moved to "AI credits" with usage-based billing, so the multiplier scheme is now its legacy system. Lovable started with "messages" at one credit per message, switched to complexity-weighted credits in 2025, and in 2026 split chat back out to a per-message price with a daily allowance. Both found that one abstract unit across tiers was the thing people kept not understanding. That shapes my answer.

**The unit.** My real opinion is that the most intuitive unit is the Expert message itself, and the abstraction only exists to charge for Basic. Basic costs under a cent a message, so I would stop charging for it: Basic is free for everyone within the 600-a-month fair use, and the only thing anyone counts or buys is Expert messages. "100 Expert messages for $10" needs no explanation, no conversion line, no two kinds of balance. The cost is a free Basic user at worst about $4 to $6 a month, at measured typical use a few cents, which fits your stated willingness to subsidise model cost for traction. Your 1:5 ratio survives as the price gap between a free message and a 10-cent one. It also deletes half the ledger: no basic-only lots, no tier multiplier, no "which coins paid for this".

If Basic stays paid, the word is **credits**, not coins. Coins say "game economy"; credits already mean "a prepaid balance you spend" to everyone, which is exactly what the pack is, and every surveyed product that tried another word ended up at credits anyway. The mapping line travels with the word wherever it first appears: "1 credit is a Basic message; an Expert message is 5." The balance is then always shown translated, "612 credits: 612 Basic or 122 Expert", because the number alone is what people cannot picture.

**The plans.** Avoid Pro, Plus and Premium: they say rank, not content, and Obico Pro already exists next door. Name them for the kind of maker, which is what the two plans really separate:

- **Hobby**, $10 a month. In my model: 150 Expert messages a month, Basic free. In yours: 750 credits.
- **Workshop**, $20 a month. In my model: 350 Expert messages a month. In yours: 1,000 credits plus unlimited Basic.

Both words are already in this audience's mouth, neither sounds like a software tier, and "Workshop" says heavy use without saying "unlimited".

**The pack.** Call the option **Pay as you go** and the thing you buy by its contents, "100 Expert messages, $10, never expire" or "500 credits". "Pack" and "bundle" sound like a one-time starter; "pay as you go" says what it is, and it is the phrase your own draft reached for. The reload toggle is "Auto-reload", your word, with its discount stated beside it.

**The free first month.** "Your first month: 100 Expert messages on us." Not "trial", which promises a wall at the end, and not "welcome coins", which needs the mapping line again.

Sources: [GitHub Copilot model multipliers, legacy billing](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-billing/request-based-billing-legacy/model-multipliers-for-annual-plans), [GitHub Copilot premium requests](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-copilot-premium-requests), [Lovable credits docs](https://docs.lovable.dev/user-guides/credits), [Lovable pricing explained](https://automationatlas.io/answers/lovable-pricing-explained-2026/), [Lovable chat pricing change, Oct 2026](https://www.usagepricing.com/blueprint/activity/lovable-2026-10-05-chat-pricing-daily-allowance).

"Per user message" divides a whole session's cost, including the turns the app starts by itself (file opened, slice finished), by the messages the person typed. ### 3.2 Charging a turn
`ledger.charge_turn(user_id, turn_id, alias, origin)`, called from `credits.admit` in place of the v1 call, inside `transaction.atomic()` with `select_for_update()` on the person's live lots:
-1. Cost = the alias's `coins` (section 3.4). Origin `app` costs 0 (section 3.3). Tier basic on an active $20 plan costs 0 until the fair-use ceiling (section 6), then 1.
+1. Cost = the alias's `credits` (section 3.4). Origin `app` costs 0 (section 3.3). Tier basic on an active $20 plan costs 0 until the fair-use ceiling (section 6), then 1.
2. Lazy trickle: if no `trickle:<this month>` lot exists for the person, create it first (section 3.5). This replaces a monthly sweep over 250k accounts.

3. Draw order: lots that expire soonest first, never-expiring lots last. Among lots with the same expiry, oldest first. `basic_only` lots are skipped for expert turns. So a sign-up lot (30 days) is spent before a subscription lot (term end), and both before a pack.

Only the first request of a turn charges, as today, so tool-call follow-ups inside a turn are free however many there are. This is what makes "per message" honest and also why the polling fix matters: follow-ups cost the gateway real money while charging nothing.

## 4. Billing: Chargebee
Reuse the two patterns Obico already runs.

-- **Packs:** plan `jusprin-coin-pack` ($0 placeholder subscription, like `pre-paid-detective-hour-pack`) with non-recurring add-on `jusprin-500-coins` at $10. `generate_coin_pack_checkout_url` copies `generate_prepaid_dhpack_checkout_url`. The `invoice_generated` webhook (status paid) creates `CoinGrant(kind=pack, source_ref=inv:<id>)`. The placeholder row that remembers the Chargebee subscription id can be a `JusPrinCoinPackPlaceholder` or a field on `JusPrinPlan`; the field is simpler.

-- **Subscriptions:** plans `jusprin-coins-10-monthly` ($10, 750 coins) and `jusprin-coins-20-monthly` ($20, 1,000 coins, unlimited basic). The existing `jusprin_cb_webhook` is extended: on `subscription_activated`, `subscription_renewed` and `subscription_changed` with status active, `CoinGrant(kind=subscription, coins=<plan's>, expires_at=current_term_end, source_ref=sub:<resource_version>:coins)` via `get_or_create`, and the `JusPrinPlan` term fields are updated. On `cancelled`, `expired_at = now`; the current lot keeps its term-end expiry so a person who cancels mid-month keeps what they paid for. No proration on plan change: the old lot expires at its own term end, the new lot is granted in full. Simpler than Obico's prorated reversal and errs in the person's favour.

-- **Obico discount** (decided: 20%): a Chargebee coupon with `duration_type = forever`, applied at checkout when `user.subscription.active()` is true locally (no live Chargebee retrieve; the v1 code's try/except around one is exactly the kind of swallowed error AGENTS.md forbids). When Obico's `upsert_subscription` handles a cancellation, it removes the coupon from any active `jusprin-coins-` subscription of that person with `Subscription.remove_coupons`. Annual JusPrin plans are not in the decided plan; if added later, the same code path works.

-- **Auto-reload with a discount** (decided, optional for the person): a flag on `JusPrinPlan` (`auto_reload`), set from the account page after a first pack purchase so a payment source exists. A Celery task, queued by `charge_turn` when the never-expiring balance drops below 50 coins and the flag is on, creates a Chargebee invoice for add-on `jusprin-500-coins-reload` at $9 (10% off) with `Invoice.create_for_charge_items_and_charges` or the site's equivalent, charged immediately; the `invoice_generated` webhook then grants the lot like any pack. Never charge inside a chat request. A failed payment turns the flag off and tells the person on the account page.

-- **Pricing page:** `web_ent/frontend/src/views/jusprin/JusPrinPricingPage.vue` is rewritten around coins, the two plans, the pack, the fair-use text (section 6) and the Obico discount. Purchases happen in the browser on Chargebee hosted pages; the desktop app opens the page, it does not embed checkout.

## 6. Fair use for unlimited basic

-Numbers: a basic message cost 0.4¢ to 1¢ normally and 5¢ when the agent polled the slicer, so the $20 plan loses money past 400 to 2,000 basic messages a month after its 1,000 coins of expert are also used. Rule (recommend):

1	# Where a person meets the credits, and how each point should feel (working doc, 2026-11-01)
2	
3	Untracked design notes, written before any coin UI is drawn or built. The pricing plan is in `pricing-implementation-plan-2026-11.md`; this document is about the person, not the ledger. It lists every point in the product where someone meets credits, says what goes wrong there in other products, and gives one opinion per point. Boards on the JusPrin v2 canvas come after Kenneth has reacted to these.
4	
5	What the survey of other products (`pricing-case-studies-2026-10.md`) says goes wrong, in one list: people cannot picture what an abstract credit buys; two kinds of credit with different expiry rules confuse everyone; the anger is at the boundary, when something they were doing stops; a balance that drops for reasons they did not cause breeds distrust; "unlimited" with an unstated ceiling is read as a lie once reached.
6	
7	## Five rules that apply at every point
8	
9	1. **One word, one unit.** "Credits", never "credits", never tokens. A coin is explained once, in messages: "an Expert message is 5 credits, a Basic message is 1". Dollars appear only on the page where money changes hands.
10	2. **Credits only move when the person sends a message.** Turns the app starts (the file-opened report, the slice-finished note) are free, and the balance never changes without a message from the person. That one fact is what makes the balance trustworthy; it is stated on the plan page in one sentence: "Only messages you send cost credits."
11	3. **Expiring credits are named by what they are, with a date. Bought credits are just "credits" and never expire.** "112 welcome credits, until 1 Dec." "50 free Basic messages this month." "450 credits." Never a bare number that mixes them. The draw rule is stated once, in the balance breakdown: "Expiring credits are used first."
12	4. **Say the number before the boundary, not at it.** Every ceiling (balance, fair use, expiry) is shown on the way there with a count, so reaching it is never news.
13	5. **Nothing typed is lost and nothing stops silently.** A message that cannot be sent stays in the composer with a way to send it anyway.
14	
15	## The points, in the order a person meets them
16	
17	### 1. First launch: own key or JusPrin account
18	
19	Where: the Agent setup in Preferences › Agent (the one setup flow, decided 2026-10-23) and the welcome screen.
20	
21	Today the choice is "your own API key" against "sign in to JusPrin", and nothing says what signing in gives. Opinion: the JusPrin row says, in one line, "Free to start: 500 credits for your first month, about 100 Expert or 500 Basic messages. Your own key stays free." No dollar figure. The first month's grant is the whole pitch at this point, so it is the one number on the screen.
22	
23	### 2. Picking Basic or Expert for a chat
24	
25	Where: the model picker in the composer (`ModelPickers.tsx`), per chat.
26	
27	Risk: "Expert, 5 credits" against "Basic, 1 coin" tells the price but not the trade. Opinion: each option gets the price and one plain clause about when to use it: "Basic · 1 coin · setting up an ordinary print" and "Expert · 5 credits · troubleshooting, tricky models, anything you'd ask a person". No model names, no vendor names: the person is choosing how much help to buy, not which company's model. The chosen tier shows on the composer as a small label, so the price of the next message is always visible before sending.
28	
29	Default for a new chat: Expert while the welcome credits last, because the first weeks decide whether the person stays. After that, the last tier the person chose.
30	
31	### 3. The balance
32	
33	Where: the composer's provider row, and Preferences › Account.
34	
35	Risk: a meter that visibly ticks down per message makes people ration and resent (Meshy, Suno); a hidden one feels like a trick when it runs out. Opinion: show the number quietly and constantly, "612 credits", with no animation and no per-message decrement flash. Hovering or tapping it opens the breakdown by kind and date (rule 3). The number changes only when the person sends a message (rule 2), so a person who watches it learns it is honest.
36	
37	Preferences › Account carries the same breakdown plus a short activity list: date, chat name, tier, credits. "Where did my credits go" has an answer the person can look up alone.
38	
39	### 4. Credits that will expire
40	
41	Where: the balance breakdown, Preferences › Account, and one notice.
42	
43	Welcome credits expire after 30 days, subscription credits at month end, the free Basic allowance at month end. Opinion: the breakdown always shows the date beside each expiring lot. One notice, seven days before a lot expires, inside the composer area once: "388 welcome credits expire on 1 Dec." Never an email for this. When the lot has expired, nothing says "you lost 388 credits"; the breakdown simply shows what remains. Losing something you did not pay for should not be dramatised.
44	
45	### 5. The next message costs more than the person has
46	
47	Where: the composer, before sending; the failed-message card if the gateway refuses anyway.
48	
49	This is the boundary where every surveyed product earns its anger. Opinion: catch it before sending. The app knows the balance and the chat's tier, so when the next Expert message cannot be paid, the Send button becomes "Send with Basic (1 coin)" and a one-line note says why: "You have 3 credits; Expert needs 5." The typed text is untouched. "Buy credits" and "Subscribe" sit next to it, not instead of it. Only a race between two sends reaches the gateway's 402, and the failed card then does the same three things with the text kept in the composer.
50	
51	Earlier than that: when the balance falls below one session's worth of the chat's tier (about 25 credits for Expert), the composer says once "About 5 Expert messages left", so the boundary is expected, not met.
52	
53	### 6. Unlimited Basic and its ceiling
54	
55	Where: the plan page, Preferences › Account, one notice in the composer.
56	
57	Risk: "unlimited" that stops at 600 reads as a lie. Opinion: never write "unlimited" alone. The plan page says "Unlimited Basic messages for one person using JusPrin by hand, up to 600 a month; after that, 1 coin each." Preferences › Account shows "412 of 600 free Basic messages this month". At 500, one notice. At 600, the composer's tier label changes to "Basic · 1 coin" with one line saying why. Nobody measured reaches 600, so this costs nothing and removes the asterisk.
58	
59	### 7. Subscription credits the person did not use
60	
61	Where: Preferences › Account; one notice; the suggestion line.
62	
63	Kenneth expects most subscribers to use under half their credits. Opinion: tell them. The month-end notice is the same as point 4 ("240 credits expire on 30 Nov"). And the "a subscription would save you money" alert runs in both directions: when a subscriber has forfeited more than half their credits two months running, the suggestion says "You used 310 credits a month lately; a 500-coin pack for $10 would last you longer." That is the trust move Kenneth described, applied to the people it costs us something to tell. It gives up some revenue from people who would otherwise churn in resentment; the measured Obico pattern is that resentment churn is the kind that never comes back.
64	
65	The alert itself (pack to subscription) appears once above the composer, dismissable, with the saving in dollars and the arithmetic one tap away ("You spent 820 credits in the last 30 days: $16.40 in packs, $10 on the monthly plan"). It is on by default and has a switch in Preferences › Account.
66	
67	### 8. Buying
68	
69	Where: the pricing page in the browser (Chargebee hosted checkout), then back in the app.
70	
71	Risk: the bounce to a browser, and the silence when the person returns ("did it go through?"). Opinion: the page has three cards and each states its expiry rule in its own words: "500 credits, $10, never expire"; "750 credits a month, $10, reset each month"; "1,000 credits a month plus unlimited Basic (up to 600), $20, reset each month". Each card also says the price in messages: "up to 100 Expert or 500 Basic messages". The Obico member price shows on the card when it applies, as the price itself, not a coupon to type. Launch double-credits shows on the pack card with its end date.
72	
73	Back in the app: the balance refreshes when the window regains focus, and the composer shows one line, "+500 credits", so the person knows it worked without opening Preferences.
74	
75	### 9. When the welcome month ends
76	
77	Where: the first launch after day 30.
78	
79	Risk: the person comes back to zero and reads it as "the free trial is over, pay up", the moment Obico's data says people leave. Opinion: the composer shows what they have, not what they lost: "50 free Basic messages this month" with the tier set to Basic. Expert is one click away and shows its price. No wall, no modal, no "upgrade" word.
80	
81	### 10. Rewards for a print report
82	
83	Where: the G-code marker in the chat and the print history, after a print.
84	
85	Opinion: show the reward before the work, in the button itself: "Tell us how it printed · 25 credits". The form says what earns it: a photo of the printed object and a few sentences. The credits land at once with a "+25 credits" line in the composer. If a report is later marked invalid, the clawback is visible in the Account activity list with a one-line reason, never a silent drop. Three rewarded reports a day; the form says so only when the person reaches it.
86	
87	### 11. Switching between own key and account
88	
89	Where: the model picker, which lists every provider the person set up.
90	
91	Opinion: credits and prices appear only on the JusPrin provider's entries. A person with both an own key and an account sees "OpenAI · gpt-5.4-mini" without a price and "JusPrin · Expert · 5 credits" with one. Nothing about credits appears anywhere for a person who never signs in.
92	
93	### 12. Obico members
94	
95	Where: the pricing page and Preferences › Account.
96	
97	Opinion: one line, "Obico member: 20% off subscriptions", shown as the price on the card and as a note in Account. It is detected, never claimed or entered.
98	
99	## What I would draw first
100	
101	Three boards on the JusPrin v2 canvas, in this order, because they carry the most risk: the composer with the tier label, balance and the pre-send "Send with Basic" state (points 2, 3, 5); Preferences › Account with the breakdown, the fair-use count and the activity list (points 3, 4, 6, 7); the pricing page's three cards (point 8). The first-launch line, the notices and the report button are copy changes on screens that exist.
102	
103	## Open for Kenneth
104	
105	- Default tier for a new chat after the welcome month: last chosen (my pick) or always Basic.
106	- The reverse alert (subscription to pack) when a subscriber forfeits over half: on (my pick) or off.
107	- Whether the balance is always visible in the composer (my pick) or only in the picker and Preferences.
108	- The word for the expiring sign-up lot: "welcome credits" (my pick), "starter credits", or "trial credits" (which I would avoid, since "trial" implies a wall at the end).

1	# JusPrin Cloud credits: implementation plan (working doc, 2026-11-01)
2	
3	Untracked working document. It turns the pricing plan Kenneth settled on 2026-11-01 into concrete work on the three codebases involved: the gateway in `tsd-enterprise` (`web_ent/jusprin/v2/`), the Obico server it is built on (`obico-server`, where the v1 credit table lives), and the desktop app (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/` and the Agent page under `AgentUI/`). Companion docs: `pricing-mental-model-2026-10.md`, `journey-cost-2026-10.md`, `obico-pro-pricing-data-2026-10.md`, `v1-pricing-data-2026-10.md`.
4	
5	Every "recommend" below is my opinion; every "decided" is Kenneth's. Code facts were read from the checkouts on 2026-11-01 (tsd-enterprise master, JusPrin `jusprin-newui` at 69780c7af4, ops master).
6	
7	## 1. The plan being implemented
8	
9	- The unit is a **coin**, about 2 cents. Credits pay per message, not per token. A **basic** message (DeepSeek V4 Flash class) costs 1 coin; an **expert** message (Claude Sonnet 5.5 class, not Opus) costs 5 credits. The 1:5 ratio is decided.
10	- **Pack:** 500 credits for $10, never expire. Optional auto-reload at a discount.
11	- **$10/month:** 750 credits, basic messages cost credits, unused credits lost at the end of each month.
12	- **$20/month:** 1,000 credits plus unlimited basic messages, unused credits lost each month. Needs fair-use wording.
13	- **Obico subscribers:** 20% off both subscriptions.
14	- **Sign-up grant:** about $10 of credits (500), expiring after one month. **Trickle:** a free monthly basic allowance for light users.
15	- **Rewards:** credits of real value for a print report with a photo and detailed text, with a human review flag for bad ones.
16	- **Launch period:** discounted, not free, credits.
17	- **Alert:** tell the person when their usage has grown to where a subscription saves them money.
18	- **BYOK** (the person's own API key) stays free with no sign-in.
19	
20	### The cost figures the margins rest on
21	
22	Measured per user message, one run per journey, from `journey-cost-2026-10.md` (Sonnet added 2026-11-01, so the peer session's "Sonnet still unmeasured" is out of date):
23	
24	| Tier | Model | Cost per user message | Price at 2¢ a coin | Gross margin |
25	|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
26	| Basic | DeepSeek V4 Flash (OpenRouter) | 0.4¢ to 1¢; 5¢ when the agent polled the slicer 75 times | 2¢ (1 coin) | 50% to 80%; negative in the polling case |
27	| Expert | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | 5.6¢ to 7.4¢, mean 6.3¢ over 14 messages | 10¢ (5 credits) | 26% to 44%, 37% at the mean |
28	| (not offered) | Claude Opus 5.5 | 10¢ to 21¢ | 10¢ | negative |
29	
30	"Per user message" divides a whole session's cost, including the turns the app starts by itself (file opened, slice finished), by the messages the person typed. So the margins above already assume app-started turns are not charged (see section 3.3). Two cost prerequisites move these: Anthropic's 5-minute cache expiry during a slow slice rewrote 72k tokens for $0.36 on Opus (section 7.1), and the slicer polling tripled one basic session (section 7.2).
31	
32	## 2. What exists today
33	
34	**Gateway.** `web_ent/jusprin/v2/gateway.py` is a raw ASGI endpoint on daphne (`tsdws-prod`) that streams `POST /ent/jusprin/v2/messages` (Anthropic format) and `/responses` (OpenAI format) to an upstream model. `credits.py` admits each turn: a Redis rate limit of 60 turns a minute per person (`JUSPRIN_V2_TURNS_PER_MINUTE`), then one v1 credit per turn through `consume_credit_for_pipeline` in `obico-server/backend/app/jusprin/ai_credits.py`, which decrements `JusPrinAICredit.ai_credit_used_current_month` against `ai_credit_free_monthly_quota` (50 a month, -1 for unlimited). A turn is every request that carries the same `X-JusPrin-Turn` header; title requests (`X-JusPrin-Request: title`) are free. The Redis keys `seen` and `charged` make the charge idempotent per turn for an hour. Exhaustion is a 402 with code `quota_exhausted`.
35	
36	**Aliases.** `aliases.py` reads `JUSPRIN_MODEL_ALIASES` (a ConfigMap, `ops/tsd/prod/jusprin-v2-gateway.yaml`). Production has one alias, `slicer-1`, label "Slicer 1", efforts fast/thorough, Anthropic backend `claude-sonnet-5-5` at 100%, OpenAI backend `gpt-6.1-sol` at 0%. Only the formats `anthropic` and `responses` exist. There is no DeepSeek backend and no image stripping.
37	
38	**Account.** `GET /jusprin/api/me/` (obico-server `JusPrinMeViewSet`) answers `{"user": {...}, "ai_credits": {...}}`; the desktop app reads only the email (`CloudAccount.cpp:233`). `GET /ent/jusprin/v2/models` lists aliases with `format`, `efforts`, `default_effort`.
39	
40	**Billing.** Chargebee, site `obico`. v1 sells `jusprin-unlimited-monthly` ($6.99) and `jusprin-unlimited-annual` ($59.99) through `web_ent/jusprin/jusprin_cb_views.py`: hosted checkout pages, a callback, a webhook that upserts `JusPrinPlan` and flips the v1 quota to -1. An Obico Pro discount coupon (30%) is applied at checkout after a live Chargebee status call. Obico's own code (`web_ent/app_ent/cb_views.py`, `detective_hour_accounting.py`) already has the two patterns the coin ledger needs: one-time packs sold as a non-recurring add-on on a placeholder subscription (`pre-paid-detective-hour-pack`, credited from the `invoice_generated` webhook, keyed `inv:<invoice id>`), and per-term included credits keyed `sub:<resource_version>:<suffix>` so a repeated webhook never double-credits. `DetectiveHourTransaction` is a ledger of signed amounts with a `forfeitable` flag; balance is a sum.
41	
42	**Obico subscriber check.** `app_ent.models.Subscription.active()` on `user.subscription`, mirrored to `user.is_pro`. Local, no Chargebee call needed.
43	
44	**Rewards precedent.** `credit_dh_for_contribution` (a Celery task) grants non-forfeitable detection hours for labelling print frames; `PrintShotFeedbackReview.invalid` is the per-label human review flag set in the admin.
45

81	
82	`ledger.charge_turn(user_id, turn_id, alias, origin)`, called from `credits.admit` in place of the v1 call, inside `transaction.atomic()` with `select_for_update()` on the person's live lots:

181	## 6. Fair use for unlimited basic
182	
183	Numbers: a basic message cost 0.4¢ to 1¢ normally and 5¢ when the agent polled the slicer, so the $20 plan loses money past 400 to 2,000 basic messages a month after its 1,000 credits of expert are also used. Rule (recommend):
184	
185	- **Ceiling:** 600 basic messages a month at no credits. Past it, a basic message costs 1 coin from the balance like on the $10 plan. 600 is 20 a day, above anything the measured sessions or v1's heaviest payer (130 chats in a month) suggest a person does by hand, and it caps the worst case at about $6 to $30 of cost on $20 of revenue.
186	- **Rate:** the existing 60 turns a minute, plus the 50 free app turns a day (3.3).
187	- **Automation:** the page says the plan is for a person using JusPrin, not for scripts or shared accounts; the ledger gives the numbers to act on, and acting is a human step through the admin, not a detector.
188	- **Page wording:** "Unlimited basic messages for one person using JusPrin by hand; after 600 in a month, basic messages cost 1 coin each. Expert messages always cost 5 credits." Say the number. Every surveyed vendor hides it and gets the anger at the boundary (mental model doc, question 2); the measured usage says 600 is a boundary almost nobody reaches, so saying it costs nothing.
189	
190	The polling fix (7.2) is what makes the 5¢ case go away; until it ships, the ceiling is the only protection.

192	## 7. The two cost prerequisites
193	
194	### 7.1 Anthropic cache lifetime
195	
196	Fact: Sonnet 5.5 cache writes cost $2.50 per million tokens for the 5-minute lifetime and $4 for one hour (fetched 2026-11-01). A session wrote 40k to 80k tokens in all, so the 1-hour lifetime adds $0.06 to $0.12 per session; one expiry after a pause over 5 minutes rewrote 42k to 72k tokens, $0.10 to $0.18 at Sonnet rates. So the 1-hour lifetime pays for itself at one real pause per session, and a person who slices, waits, reads and types pauses more than that.
197	
198	Where (recommend): the gateway, not the app. `upstream.py`'s `prepare()` already parses the Anthropic body; it adds `"ttl": "1h"` to every `cache_control` block for the `anthropic` backend. That keeps the pricing lever on the server, ships without an app release, and BYOK users keep paying Anthropic's default on their own key. Anthropic requires 1-hour breakpoints to come before 5-minute ones in the prompt; setting all three to 1h satisfies that. Verify on the live gateway by comparing `cache_creation_input_tokens` across a turn separated by a 10-minute pause, before and after.
199	
200	The slice-finished turn itself no longer rewrites the prefix since the append-only record landed (commit 1635438d4f); the 1-hour lifetime covers the slice taking longer than 5 minutes.
201	
202	### 7.2 Stop the agent polling the slicer
203	
204	Two steps, the small one first:
205	
206	1. **Guard in the host** (`ToolExecutionCoordinator`): while a slice the agent started in this turn is running, a `workspace_inspect` that asks for `slicing`, or a `slice_report`, is answered with the tool error code `busy` and the message "The slice is still running. This turn has nothing left to do: the app starts a new turn with the outcome. Finish your reply." After the third such refusal in one turn the host ends the turn (the same path as the person's Stop) and the slice-finished note turn carries on. `busy` is in the one error-code list (`Agent/ToolErrors.hpp`), and a waiting slice is an expected state, so this is normal control flow, not a swallowed error. Each refused call still costs one small request, so three is the cap on the waste.
207	2. **End the turn at `slice_start`** (the real fix, later): when `slice_start` returns `started: true`, the host closes the turn instead of returning the result to the model, and the slice-finished note turn carries both the `tool_result` for that call and the note text in one user message. The model never gets a chance to poll, the person sees the model's text before the tool plus the slice card, and the follow-up request happens once. This touches `ProviderAgent`'s turn continuation and both codecs (a deferred tool result), so it is its own piece of work with the tool-pairing rules of both wire formats tested.
208	
209	The measured waste was two thirds of a basic session's cost on a debug build; a shipped build slices faster so the poll count is lower, but the fix removes the behaviour rather than the opportunity.

253	6. **Reward size:** 25 credits per accepted report, three a day (recommend); 10 to 20 was the range in the draft.
254	7. **Launch discount form:** double credits on packs by server flag (recommend) or a Chargebee coupon.
255	8. **v1 unlimited subscribers:** treated as the $20 plan until term end (recommend).
256	9. **Pix and BRL pricing:** verify Chargebee's support on this site before promising it.
257	10. **Domain:** still open from the gateway rollout; the pricing page URL the app opens moves with it.
258
